u$ distinct points, and put $U=X\setminus S$. A discrete group with loops of type $(g,
u)$ consists of a group $\pi$, a finite index set $I$ of cardinality $
u$, a free rank-one integral orientation module $T$, and exterior homomorphisms $\kappa_i:T	o\pi$. Here an exterior homomorphism is a conjugacy class, under conjugation in the target, of actual homomorphisms. After choosing a generator of $T$, representatives $c_i=\kappa_i(1)$, an ordering of $I$, and the handle generators, these data admit the presentation \[ \pi_{g,

When $I$ is empty one additionally identifies $T$ with the dual of $H^2(\pi;\Z)$, or its continuous profinite counterpart. This is the covariant orientation convention of scan 116. More precisely, an earlier cohomological marking $\kappa:H^2(\pi;\Z)\xrightarrow{\sim}T_{\mathrm{coh}}$ on scan 91 gives, by dualization, $\kappa^\vee:T_{\mathrm{coh}}^\vee\xrightarrow{\sim}H_2(\pi;\Z)$; the covariant module used here is $T=T_{\mathrm{coh}}^\vee$. The same typed dual map specifies the profinite convention. For an isomorphism of groups with loops the data are an isomorphism $f:\pi	o\pi_1$, a bijection $s:I	o I_1$, and an isomorphism $t:T	o T_1$ such that $f\kappa_i$ is conjugate to $\kappa_{s(i)}t$ for every $i$, with the corresponding dual-cohomology compatibility when $I$ is empty. An exterior group with loops regards two such $f$ as equivalent when they differ by target inner conjugation, with the same $s,t$. Thus its isomorphism sets are explicitly the quotient of the preceding isomorphism sets by $\Inn(\pi_1)$. In all nontrivial admitted types $L_i=\kappa_i(T)$ recovers its source by A.2; the one-puncture sphere requires the original source map. For $

The same list holds for their profinite completions. The peripheral maps from the source orientation group $\Z$ to $\pi$ are injective except at $(0,1)$, among the types admitted in scans 91--92. statement: Discrete peripheral rigidity in every hyperbolic type — For $2g+\nu>2$, the group $\pi=\pi_{g,\nu}$ has trivial centre and $C_\pi(H)=1$ for every finite-index subgroup $H$. For every peripheral subgroup and every integer $n\ge1$, \[ N_\pi(L_i)=C_\pi(L_i)=C_\pi(L_i^n)=L_i. \] Distinct peripheral indices give distinct, noncommensurable conjugacy classes.

statement: Exact exceptional-case table — The discrete and profinite exceptional groups have the following properties; in the profinite column replace $\Z$ by $\widehat\Z$. \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c} (g,\nu)&\pi& Z(\pi)&C_\pi(H)\ (H\text{ finite index/open})&\text{peripherals}\\\hline (0,0)&1&1&1&\text{none}\\ (0,1)&1&1&1&L_1=1\\ (0,2)&\Z&\Z&\Z&L_1=L_2=\pi\\ (1,0)&\Z^2&\Z^2&\Z^2&\text{none} \end{array} \] Consequently the peripheral normalizer and power-centralizer equalities hold in the plane and annulus, while distinctness of the two peripheral classes fails on the annulus. The nonzero vector $1$ on the annulus and $(1,0)$ on the torus witness failure of both centre and finite-index-centralizer assertions. The plane's failure is the noninjective source map, not a nontrivial centre. For the standard base-element formula of scan 501, the annulus satisfies the equality since its basis element generates its whole group. On the torus $C(\langle(1,0)\rangle^n)=\Z^2$ for every $n\ge1$, and $(0,1)$ witnesses its failure to equal $\langle(1,0)\rangle$. The same vector works after completion. The sphere and plane have no nontrivial base elements to test.

statement: Peripheral decomposition groups and transporters — Let $1\to\pi\to E\xrightarrow{p}\Gamma\to1$ arise from an action on a hyperbolic marked surface. Choose one peripheral subgroup $L_s$ and the corresponding peripheral lift group $E_s\subset E$; thus $E_s\cap\pi=L_s$ and $p(E_s)=\Gamma_s$, the stabilizer of that puncture. Define \[ \operatorname{Trans}_E(L_s^d,L_s) =\{e\in E:eL_s^de^{-1}\subseteq L_s\}\qquad(d\ge1). \] Then $N_E(L_s)=\operatorname{Trans}_E(L_s^d,L_s)=E_s$. The same assertions hold for the corresponding profinite extension and closed peripheral groups. On the annulus these assertions fail for $z\mapsto1/z$: with $E=\Z\rtimes C_2$ and the involution acting by inversion, $E_s=\Z$ but $N_E(L_s)=E$ and every transporter is $E$. More generally for every annulus action both normalizer and transporter equal $E$, while $E_s$ is the inverse image of the end stabilizer. Thus their equality with $E_s$ holds exactly when the action fixes both ends. On the one-puncture sphere the peripheral mixed group maps onto $E=\Gamma$ with kernel $\Z$; using its image, both equalities hold, whereas identifying that mixed group itself with a subgroup is invalid. The closed sphere and torus have no peripheral statement.

statement: Centre-free extension reconstruction and its abelian correction — For a centre-free discrete group $\pi$ and a homomorphism $\rho:\Gamma\to\Out(\pi)$, the extension inducing $\rho$ is, up to a unique isomorphism inducing the identity on its prescribed kernel and quotient, \[ E_\rho=\{(a,\gamma)\in\Aut(\pi)\times\Gamma:[a]=\rho(\gamma)\}. \] The same formula holds for a topologically finitely generated centre-free profinite $\pi$ and continuous $\rho$, with the profinite topology. For $A=\Z$ or $\Z^2$ and a prescribed action $\rho:\Gamma\to\Aut(A)$, extension classes with their kernel and quotient identified are instead classified by $H^2(\Gamma;A_\rho)$. Their automorphisms inducing the identity on both ends form $Z^1(\Gamma;A_\rho)$. For finite $\Gamma$ this statement holds with $A=\widehat\Z$ or $\widehat\Z^2$ and continuous cochains. Thus both the annulus and the torus require the abelian correction.

statement: The full profinite rigidity statements, with reductions — For the full profinite completion $\Pi=\widehat\pi_{g,\nu}$ of a hyperbolic type, $\Pi$ is torsion-free, $C_\Pi(H)=1$ for every open subgroup $H$, and \[ N_\Pi(\widehat L_i)=C_\Pi(\widehat L_i^n)=\widehat L_i \quad(n\in\Z_{>0}). \] Distinct peripheral classes are noncommensurable. The same conclusions hold for the pro-$p$ completions, for every prime $p$, including $2$ and $3$. The four exceptional types have exactly the completed table of A.4, and A.5 supplies the extension and transporter assertions.

statement: Lemme 5 from open-subgroup centralizers alone — Let $P$ be a discrete or profinite group for which the centralizer of every finite-index, respectively open, subgroup is trivial. Let $H\subset P$ be such a subgroup and let $u\in\Aut(P)$ preserve $H$. An automorphism restricting to the identity on $H$ is the identity on $P$. An automorphism whose restriction equals $\operatorname{conj}_h$ for some $h\in H$ equals $\operatorname{conj}_h$ on $P$.

statement: Faithfulness ascends along a finite etale cover — Let $k$ be a characteristic-zero field, $U/k$ a hyperbolic geometrically connected smooth curve, and $V\to U$ a finite etale geometrically connected covering defined over $k$. Put $\Gamma=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline k/k)$ and choose compatible geometric base points. Faithfulness of $\Gamma\to\Out(\pi_1(U_{\overline k}))$ implies faithfulness of $\Gamma\to\Out(\pi_1(V_{\overline k}))$.

Then $\Lambda\simeq\widehat\Z$ and, for every positive integer $n$, \[ C_\Pi(\Lambda^n)=N_\Pi(\Lambda^n)=\Lambda. \]

statement: What the abstract profinite presentation specifies — The full profinite presentation required by scan 318, equation (4), already determines a profinite group with loops isomorphic to $\widehat\pi_{g,\nu}$ with its standard loops. Hence A.7 and A.10 apply to every abstract object satisfying that presentation axiom. Merely requiring generators to satisfy the displayed equation would not suffice: $P=\widehat\Z^2$, $c_1=(1,0)$, $c_2=(0,1)$, $c_3=(-1,-1)$ satisfies the $(0,3)$ relation, has three injective procyclic peripheral subgroups and the rank-one orientation kernel, but has centre $P$.

The discrete filling isomorphism and all compatibility maps — Let $U=X\setminus S$ be hyperbolic, choose $b\in U$, and put $U'=U\setminus\{b\}$, $\pi'=\pi_1(U')$, and $\pi=\pi'/\langle\!\langle L_bangle\!angle$. Choose the peripheral representative $L_b\subset\pi'$. The normalization of representatives defines an isomorphism of discrete groups \[ d_b:\Out_{\mathrm{lac}}(\pi';b)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Aut_{\mathrm{lac}}(\pi). \] On both sides old punctures may be permuted and orientation may be reversed. It identifies the pure orientation-preserving subgroups, whose common index is $2

statement: Filling into the two abelian targets — Exactly one of the drilled and filled groups is abelian in the two cases $(0,3)\to(0,2)$ and $(1,1)\to(1,0)$. In the first, the homomorphism on automorphisms of the underlying groups with peripheral subgroup classes is \[ C_2\times C_2=\Out_{\mathrm{lac}}(F_2;[\langle xy\rangle]) \longrightarrow\Aut(\Z)=C_2, \] with kernel of order two. Its nontrivial element has representative $x\mapsto y^{-1}$, $y\mapsto x^{-1}$. Its restriction to the positive-orientation subgroup is an isomorphism. Retaining the two indexed peripheral source maps and their orientation line on the annulus enlarges the target automorphism group to $C_2\times C_2$ and restores the full isomorphism. In the second case the filling map is the isomorphism $\operatorname{GL}_2(\Z)\to\operatorname{GL}_2(\Z)$, with positive subgroup $\operatorname{SL}_2(\Z)$.

statement: Primitive loops in finite-step solvable quotients — Let $\Sigma$ be a nonempty set of primes, $F$ a free pro-$\Sigma$ group of finite rank at least two, and $F^{[j]}$ its closed derived series. Put $F_m=F/F^{[m]}$, $m\ge2$. For any element $x$ of a free basis and any positive integer $n$, \[ C_{F_m}(x^n)=N_{F_m}(\overline{\langle x\rangle}) =\overline{\langle x\rangle}\simeq\Z_\Sigma, \qquad \Z_\Sigma=\prod_{p\in\Sigma}\Z_p. \] Every open subgroup of $F_m$ has trivial centralizer. For $\nu\ge2$, all peripheral loops of the pro-$\Sigma$ group of type $(g,\nu)$ satisfy these formulas in every $F_m$. Their indexed conjugacy classes are pairwise distinct in all hyperbolic types.

statement: The one-puncture solvable threshold, with a finite certificate — Let $F$ be the pro-$\Sigma$ completion of $\pi_{g,1}$, $g\ge1$, let $c=\prod_{j=1}^g[a_j,b_j]$ (the inverse peripheral generator), and write $c$ for its image in $F_m=F/F^{[m]}$. For every positive integer $n$, \[ \begin{array}{ll} m=2:& C_{F_2}(c^n)=N_{F_2}(\overline{\langle c\rangle})=F_2',\\[2pt] m\ge3:&C_{F_m}(c^n)=N_{F_m}(\overline{\langle c\rangle}) =\overline{\langle c\rangle}. \end{array} \] In the first line the inclusion $\overline{\langle c\rangle}\subset F_2'$ is strict. Thus peripheral rigidity fails at the smallest solvable depth $m=2$ and is restored at every $m\ge3$, for the full profinite and every pro-$p$ version.

For every $m\ge2$, $P_m$ is torsion-free and centre-free. This verifies the form of \cite[Theorem 2.9 and Corollary 2.10]{A_Yamaguchi2026} needed here by the following argument from finite covers and transfer.

statement:
The remaining affine solvable rigidity list and a closed bound — For all hyperbolic types with $
u>0$, and all $m\ge2$, the maximal $m$-step-solvable full profinite or pro-$\Sigma$ quotient has trivial centre and trivial centralizers of open subgroups, and is torsion-free. Peripheral conjugacy classes remain distinct. For $
u\ge2$ all peripheral normalizer and integer-power-centralizer equalities hold at every $m\ge2$; for $
u=1$ their exact values are those of A.16. In an extension obtained by quotienting a geometric action extension by the $m$th closed derived subgroup of its kernel, the equality $N_E(L_s)=E_s$ holds in the former cases and at $m\ge3$ in the latter. At $
u=1,m=2$ its correct value is $N_E(L_s)=F_2'E_s$, with the intersection $F_2'\cap E_s=L_s$. In all these cases every transporter $\operatorname{Trans}_E(L_s^d,L_s)$, $d\ge1$, equals the same displayed normalizer. Since the kernels are centre-free by A.17, the extension reconstruction of A.6 also applies to all these solvable quotients. Standard free-basis generators satisfy the power-centralizer formula at every $m\ge2$ by A.14. For a closed hyperbolic group $P$ and an open subgroup $H\subset P_m$, the proven universal bound is \[ C_{P_m}(H)\subseteq P_m^{[m-1]}. \]

statement: Closed finite-step power centralizers and slimness — Let $P$ be the pro-$\Sigma$ completion of a closed oriented surface group of genus $g\ge2$, let $m\ge2$, and put $P_m=P/P^{[m]}$. Let $x$ be represented by a nonseparating simple closed curve, in particular by any standard handle generator. Then for every positive integer $n$, \[ C_{P_m}(x^n)=N_{P_m}(\overline{\langle x^n\rangle}) =\overline{\langle x\rangle}\simeq\Z_\Sigma. \] Consequently $C_{P_m}(H)=1$ for every open subgroup $H$. This includes the full profinite and every pro-$p$ quotient, without a restriction at $p=2$ or $3$.

statement: The typed completion comparison for filling — For the two hyperbolic groups in A.12, put $\Pi'=\widehat{\pi'}$ and $\Pi=\widehat\pi$. There is a commutative diagram of profinite groups \[ \begin{array}{ccc} \widehat{\Out_{\mathrm{lac}}(\pi';b)} &\xrightarrow{\ \widehat{d_b}\ }& \widehat{\Aut_{\mathrm{lac}}(\pi)}\\ \big\downarrow c_{\mathrm{out}}&&\big\downarrow c_{\mathrm{aut}}\\ \Out_{\mathrm{lac}}(\Pi';b) &\xrightarrow{\ d_b^{\mathrm{cont}}\ }& \Aut_{\mathrm{lac}}(\Pi). \end{array} \] The upper horizontal map is an isomorphism. The lower horizontal map is the normalized filling homomorphism on all continuous loop automorphisms. The vertical maps are induced by extending discrete automorphisms to group completions. The same construction with pro-$p$ completions of the surface groups still has the full profinite completions of the discrete automorphism groups in its upper row. These assertions specify the precise consequence of the discrete filling theorem; no isomorphism assertion for the lower horizontal or vertical arrows is used.

statement: Finite plane actions and simultaneous local models — Every faithful action of a finite group $H$ on $\R^2$ by homeomorphisms is conjugate to an orthogonal action. When $H^+\ne1$, $H^+$ is cyclic, $H$ is cyclic or dihedral, and $(\R^2)^H$ is a single point. A nontrivial orientation-reversing involution has a fixed line. Every stabilizer in a finite action on a surface with universal cover $\R^2$ has an invariant disc on which the whole stabilizer acts by an orthogonal action. These conclusions supply the two local assertions used in \S15, folios 70--74, scans 141--149, and \S33, scan 440.

statement: The omitted orientation hypothesis in scans 146--147 — The displayed lemma on scan 147, taken without its preceding orientation hypothesis, is false. Its correct form is: an orientation-preserving finite-order homeomorphism $u$ of $\C$ commuting with $T(z)=z+1$ and satisfying $u(0)=0$ is the identity. The quotient $\C/\Z$ provides a complete proof along the route proposed in the manuscript.

statement: Sections and isolated fixed points — Let $\widetilde U\cong\R^2$. A faithful finite action on $U$ with $G^+\ne1$ has a bijection \[ U^G\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sec}(E\to G)/\pi. \] For every section subgroup $K$, $C_\pi(K)=1$. Existence of a section forces $G$ to be cyclic or dihedral. More generally, every nontrivial finite subgroup of $E$ whose orientation-preserving part is nontrivial is contained in exactly one maximal finite subgroup of $E$. For an orientation-preserving action the map from points with nontrivial stabilizer to maximal partial-section classes is a $G$-equivariant bijection. These are the theorem and corollary of \S15, folios 73--75, scans 148--151, with their stated orientation hypotheses.
where_proved: Paper, Part B, statement B.3; computation locations are specified in that proof.

statement: Reflection sections, ovals, and punctured ovals — Let $\sigma$ be an orientation-reversing involution of $U$ with $\widetilde U\cong\R^2$, and let $E\to C_2$ be its lift extension. There is a bijection \[ \pi_0(U^\sigma)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sec}(E\to C_2)/\pi. \] For the section $s$ associated with a component $Z$, inclusion induces an isomorphism $\pi_1(Z)\cong C_\pi(s)$. Thus the centralizer is $1$ for a line and $\Z$ for an oval. This includes punctures fixed or permuted by $\sigma$ and proves \S33, folios 222--225, scans 440--445, in the required noncompact cases.
where_proved: Paper, Part B, statement B.4; computation locations are specified in that proof.

statement: Recovering the incidence and cyclic order of real punctures — For a hyperbolic $U=X\setminus S$ with anti-involution $\sigma$, its discrete extension together with its indexed peripheral subgroups determines the following finite graph. Its vertices are the section classes of B.4, its edges are the real punctures, and each edge is attached to its two adjacent real half-branches. Every punctured oval gives one cycle, allowing a loop or two parallel edges. The graph recovers which punctures lie on each oval and their cyclic order up to reversal. Unpunctured ovals are the vertices with infinite cyclic centralizer. The claim uses the extension and peripheral incidence maps; a naked set of section classes alone has no such incidence information.

statement: The fundamental loop lemma of \S18 — Let $\pi=\pi_1(U)$ be hyperbolic and discrete, with its indexed peripheral structure and orientation module. A finite-order orientation-preserving automorphism of $\pi$ fixing a peripheral index and normalizing its subgroup $L_i$ is the identity. Consequently the peripheral extension attached to a nontrivial finite-order positive outer automorphism fixing $i$ cannot split. This proves the lemma and corollary of scans 193--194 without adding realizability to the hypotheses.

statement: The unrestricted fixed-subgroup question, with its replacement — The assertion $\pi^G=1$ for every finite $G\le\Aut_{\rm lac}(\pi)$ is false. For a hyperbolic discrete $\pi$, a nontrivial finite genuine loop action has fixed subgroup $1$ when its positive part is nontrivial. Its remaining possibility is a reflection action of $C_2$; its fixed subgroup is $1$ or $\Z$, as in B.4. For any finite-type faithful geometric action there are finitely many classes of full and partial sections. This answers questions (c) and (e), scans 197--198.

statement: An intrinsic discrete formula for the multiplier — For a geometric finite extension of a hyperbolic discrete surface group, $E$ with its peripheral structure and orientation module $T$ determines $\mu_E$ on all torsion elements. On $E^+$ it is the rotation number of its canonical oriented boundary action. More explicitly, let $\widetilde{\operatorname{Homeo}}^+(S^1)\to\operatorname{Homeo}^+(S^1)$ be the central extension by the positively oriented deck translation $z$. For $u\in E^+$ of order $n$ and any lift $\widetilde u$, write $\widetilde u^{,n}=z^k$. Then \[ \mu_E(u)=\frac{k}{n}\pmod{\Z}\quad\hbox{in }T\otimes\Q/\Z. \] For a nonidentity orientation-reversing torsion element we put $\mu_E(u)$ equal to the unique nonzero element of order two. With this convention the formula is natural under isomorphisms preserving the loops and transporting $T$, satisfies $\mu(u^m)=m\mu(u)$, and has the same order as $u$. This answers the discrete intrinsicity question of \S15, folios 77--79, scans 155--160.

statement: Finite annulus and torus actions, and their multipliers — Every finite topological action on the torus is topologically conjugate to an affine action on $V/\Lambda$, where $\Lambda\cong\Z^2$ and $V=\Lambda\otimes\R$. For a fixed finite operator group $G$ such an action is specified by a homomorphism $A:G\to GL(\Lambda)$ and a cocycle $b\in Z^1(G,V/\Lambda)$, subject to faithfulness of $g\mapsto(x\mapsto A_gx+b_g)$. Translation conjugacy corresponds exactly to a coboundary, and \[ H^1(G,V/\Lambda)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^2(G,\Lambda) \] is the connecting homomorphism. Linear changes of the lattice give the further conjugacies. Every finite annulus action has a simultaneous normal form \[ (x,t)\longmapsto(\epsilon_g x+a_g,\eta_g t), \qquad x\in\R/\Z,\quad t\in\R,\quad \epsilon_g,\eta_g\in\{1,-1\}. \] These descriptions determine the multiplier of every finite-order element in the respective lift extensions.

statement: Complete topological classification of anti-involutions — Conjugacy classes of anti-involutions of a closed oriented genus-$g$ surface are classified by the orientability of the quotient and its number $b$ of boundary components. The possibilities are \[ \begin{array}{ll} \text{nonorientable quotient:}&0\le b\le g,\quad h=g+1-b\ge1\text{ crosscaps};\\ \text{orientable quotient:}&b\ge1,\quad g=2h+b-1,\quad h\ge0. \end{array} \] There are $(g+1)+\lfloor(g+2)/2\rfloor=\lfloor(3g+4)/2\rfloor$ classes. For $\nu$ unlabelled invariant punctures the additional data are an integer $r\ge0$ and an unordered list $(q_1,\ldots,q_b)$ of nonnegative integers with $2r+\sum q_i=\nu$: $r$ is the number of interior punctures of the quotient, and $q_i$ counts punctures on its $i$th boundary circle.

statement: The two centralizer corollaries in both quotient families — Let $g\ge2$, and let an anti-involution of $X_g$ have $b>0$ ovals, with outer class $\sigma$. There are exactly $b$ classes of order-two genuine loop automorphisms lifting $\sigma$, under conjugacy by $\pi_g$. For each lift $u$, $\pi_g^u\cong\Z$. The positive centralizer of $\sigma$ acts transitively on those $b$ classes. More precisely, writing $A=\Aut_{\rm lac}(\pi_g)$ and $O=\Out_{\rm lac}(\pi_g)$, there is an exact sequence \[ 1\longrightarrow\pi_g^u\longrightarrow C_{A^+}(u) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Stab}_{C_{O^+}(\sigma)}([u])\longrightarrow1, \] and the last group has index $b$ in $C_{O^+}(\sigma)$. The corresponding full centralizer image also has index $b$. This proves Corollaries 1 and 2, folios 225--226, scans 445--448, for both orientable and nonorientable quotients.

statement: The tube twists, their maximality property, and their normalizer — For $g\ge2$, the elements $\rho_j$ of \S33, scans 453--470, are full Dehn twists about a cut system $c_1,\ldots,c_g$: disjoint nonseparating curves with connected complement. They generate $H\cong\Z^g$. This is not a maximal free abelian subgroup of $\mathcal T_g$: it is contained in a multitwist subgroup of rank $3g-3$. It has the precise maximality property of being a full multitwist group of largest rank whose supporting multicurve has connected complement. Furthermore \[ N_{\mathcal T_g}(H)=\operatorname{Stab}_{\mathcal T_g}(\{c_1,\ldots,c_g\}), \qquad N_{\mathcal T_g}(H)/C_{\mathcal T_g}(H)\cong S_g\times C_2. \] The action on $H$ permutes its basis and multiplies every basis vector by the same orientation sign. Cutting and capping gives an exact sequence \[ 1\longrightarrow H\longrightarrow N_{\mathcal T_g}(H) \longrightarrow\mathcal T^{\rm pairs}_{0,2g}\longrightarrow1, \] where the last extended sphere mapping class group preserves the partition of its $2g$ punctures into the $g$ unordered gluing pairs.

statement: Relations for arbitrary strips and a uniform obstruction to generation — Choose for each $c_j$ one simple transversal $d_j$, using a strip in the complement of the other tubes, so that $i(c_i,d_j)=\delta_{ij}$. Its supported subgroup is the central extension $\langle A_j,B_j\rangle\cong B_3$ of B.21, with quotient $SL_2(\Z)$. In those coordinates, \[ \widetilde{\mathcal C}_O=D_1\times D_2,\qquad \mathcal C_O\cong(D_1\times D_2)/\Delta,\qquad O/\mathcal C_O\cong\R^2/(D_1\times D_2). \tag{C.57.2} \] All these are topological-group or quotient-space identifications through the original covering. Up to exchange of coordinates, the final quotient is \[ \begin{array}{c|c|c} D_1\times D_2& O/\mathcal C_O &\text{compact}\\ \hline 1&\R^2&\text{no}\\ \Z\times1&S^1\times\R&\text{no}\\ \R\times1&\R&\text{no}\\ \Z^2&S^1\times S^1&\text{yes}\\ \R\times\Z&S^1&\text{yes}\\ \R^2&\{\ast\}&\text{yes}. \end{array} \tag{C.57.3} \] For the half-plane domain, $\Delta=1$ and $\mathcal C_O=1$, so its quotient is a plane. For the band domain $D=\{x<y<x+1\}$, put $e(x,y)=(y,x+1)$. Then \[ \widetilde{\mathcal C}_O=\langle e\rangle\cong\Z,\qquad \Delta=1\ \text{or}\ \langle e^{2m}\rangle\ (m\geq1), \qquad \mathcal C_O\cong\langle e\rangle/\Delta. \tag{C.57.4} \] Its quotient $O/\mathcal C_O$ is always the open M\"obius band. Thus every noncocompact case in this two-family list has full lifted local centralizer $1$, $\Z$, or $\R$, with quotient a plane, open cylinder, line, or open M\"obius band. This identifies the groups and quotient maps; it asserts no further contraction at their frontiers.

statement: All-prime dihedral compatibility and the multiplier-one obstruction — The inverse limit $D$ over all the dihedral levels of D.24 has the following explicit isomorphism of profinite groups: \[ D\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } \left(\prod_{p\text{ odd}}\operatorname{Aff}(\Z_p)\right) \times H_2. \tag{D.25a} \] There is a canonical continuous homomorphism $GT_0\to D$. Put $F=\widehat F_2=\langle x,y\rangle$ and define the continuous epimorphism and its closed kernel by \[ \kappa:F\longrightarrow\prod_pF_2^{(p)},\qquad R=\ker\kappa. \] Write $\lambda:GT_0\to\widehat\Z^\times$ for the multiplier. Extend it to $\widetilde\chi:E\to C_m$ by $\widetilde\chi(v)=0$, and put $F_m=\ker\chi$, $E_m=\ker\widetilde\chi$. statement: LM4-F.b, the intrinsic open-image statement — Let $M\leq B$ be an oriented geometric subgroup, $H=\overline M$, $N=N_B(H)$, and let $i:G\hookrightarrow H$ be a fixed finite embedding. statement: LM4-F.c: the exact canonical lift of a section stabilizer — Let $\pi$ be a centre-free discrete surface group or its full profinite completion, and put \[ A=\Aut_{\rm lac}(\pi),\qquad B=\Out_{\rm lac}(\pi). \] Let $G\leq B$ be finite and let $s:G\to A$ be a specified lift with $C_\pi(s(G))=1$. The natural map \[ C_A(s(G))\longrightarrow C_B(G) \] is injective. Its image is the stabilizer of the $\pi$-conjugacy class $[s]$ in the set of lifts of the labelled inclusion $G\hookrightarrow B$. Its inverse is the canonical homomorphism lifting that stabilizer to $A$ and centralizing $s(G)$. In the profinite case it is continuous. For geometrically realized actions with a nontrivial rotation the section-class set is finite, so this stabilizer has finite index and is open in the profinite case.
